nature-res-033.title: Fisheries: where people meet wild fish
nature-res-033.text: About 500 million people worldwide depend on fisheries for their living. A fishery is either the business of catching or raising fish and other aquatic life or, more often, the place where it happens, the fishing grounds. The FAO defines it as any activity leading to harvesting fish, wild-caught or farmed. In this world 'fish' is a collective word that includes molluscs, crustaceans and any aquatic animal harvested for economic value. A fishery is usually defined by its people, species, area, fishing method, class of boats and purpose. Close to 90% of catches come from oceans and seas, mostly near coasts, where nutrients make fish abundant. Total fish production hit a record 171 million tonnes in 2016, and 88% of it was eaten directly by people. A 2014 estimate put fisheries' contribution to global GDP at US$270 billion a year, with up to US$50 billion more possible from fully sustainable fishing. Fisheries were once 'first-come, first-served'. Catching fish faster than they could breed has forced more and more regulation.

nature-res-038.title: Aquaculture: farming the water
nature-res-038.text: In 2014, farmed fish overtook wild fish as human food. Aquaculture, or aquafarming, is the controlled farming of aquatic organisms such as fish, crustaceans, molluscs, algae and aquatic plants. Unlike commercial fishing, which harvests wild fish, it raises freshwater, brackish and saltwater populations under controlled conditions. Wild harvests have been static since the late 1980s while demand for protein grew, raising hopes of a 'Blue Revolution'. In 2016 aquaculture made up 47 percent of the 171 million tonnes of fish produced. Farming creates private stocks, which gives farmers a reason to conserve them. Shellfish farming adds filter feeders that can significantly improve water quality. Other farming does harm. Salmon and other carnivorous fish eat fishmeal and fish oil from wild forage fish, so farming them does not relieve wild stocks. Shrimp farming helped destroy about 20 percent of mangrove forests since 1980, and a 200,000-salmon farm discharges more fecal waste than a city of 60,000.

nature-res-049.title: Fish stocks: the unit fisheries manage
nature-res-049.text: Fish tend to form partly separate populations that breed mostly among themselves, so fishing one may leave its neighbor untouched. A fish stock is such a subpopulation of one species. Its growth, arrival of young fish and deaths, including from fishing, are treated as the main drivers of its numbers. Fisheries scientists define it as a semi-discrete group of fish with attributes of interest to managers. The trend is worrying. The FAO found that stocks fished within biologically sustainable levels fell from 90% in 1974 to 62.3% in 2021. A 2020 FAO report classed 34% of the world's marine fish stocks as overfished. Stocks of different species can move together: as Atlantic blue marlin catches fell in the 1960s, sailfish catches rose. Their health is tracked under {{ref:nature-gov-027}} by indicator 14.4.1.

nature-res-027.title: Overfishing: taking fish faster than they breed
nature-res-027.text: Fish and marine mammal biomass has fallen by 60% since the 1800s, largely through overfishing. Overfishing is taking fish from a body of water faster than the species can replace itself, so its numbers there keep falling. It can happen anywhere, from ponds and rivers to oceans, and it leaves depleted populations, slower growth and low biomass. The trend is steep. The share of stocks within biologically sustainable levels fell from 90% in 1974 to 66.9% in 2015. The FAO reported 34 percent of marine stocks overfished in 2017. Illegal catch adds an estimated 11 to 26 million tonnes, 14–33% of the world's reported catch. Pushed far enough, a population may no longer sustain itself, a state called critical depensation, and it is wiped out locally or globally. Collapsed stocks may not return. After trout are overfished, carp can take over and stop trout re-establishing. Remedies include regulation, removing subsidies, gentler fishing gear, fish farming and consumer awareness.

nature-res-001.title: Fisheries management: rules for a renewable catch
nature-res-001.text: Norway passed a law on its Lofoten fishery in 1816, and some fisheries have been managed for hundreds of years. Fisheries management is the set of tasks that guide users and managers toward the best use of renewable aquatic resources, mainly fish. Wild stocks count as renewable when they produce a yearly surplus that can be harvested without lowering future productivity. The goal is lasting biological, environmental and economic benefit. The FAO admits there is no generally accepted definition. Its working one covers gathering information, planning, deciding, making rules and enforcing them. Modern management is often a government system of rules based on set objectives, enforced through monitoring, control and surveillance. In Europe, government action to protect fish stocks began after the first Overfishing Conference in London in 1936. The stakes are large: a 2008 World Bank and FAO report put the loss from depleted stocks and poor management at US$50 billion a year. The fisheries scientist Milo Adkison argues that the main limit on good decisions is a lack of good-quality data.

nature-res-008.title: Sustainable fisheries: catching without shrinking the stock
nature-res-008.text: Over 70% of fish species are fully exploited, overexploited, depleted or recovering from depletion. A sustainable fishery is conventionally one harvested at a rate at which the fish population does not decline over time because of fishing. It joins theory, such as population dynamics, with practice: quotas, curbing illegal fishing, {{ref:nature-res-024}} and certification. The worries run beyond lost yield. Stocks can lose diversity and resilience, swing through boom-and-bust cycles, and be fished down marine food webs. The stakes are human. Fisheries and fish farming support the livelihoods of over 500 million people, mostly in developing countries. Yet sustainable fisheries made up only about 0.1 per cent of global GDP in 2017, according to a 2021 UN report. Global wild catches are believed to have peaked and begun to decline.

nature-res-013.title: Maximum sustainable yield: the biggest catch forever
nature-res-013.text: A small fish population grows slowly, because few fish breed. A population near its carrying capacity also barely grows, because crowding stops it. In between lies a sweet spot where the yearly surplus is largest. Maximum sustainable yield (MSY) is, in theory, the largest catch that can be taken from a stock year after year for an indefinite period. It keeps a population at the size where it grows fastest and harvests the individuals that would otherwise be added. In the logistic model that size is half the carrying capacity; modern fisheries models put it nearer 30% of the unexploited population. MSY is usually higher than the catches that maximize economic returns, {{ref:nature-res-060}} and {{ref:nature-res-084}}. It became popular in the 1950s and was adopted as the main goal by bodies such as the International Whaling Commission (IWC) and the tuna commission ICCAT. A 1955 international treaty built on MSY let foreign fleets fish off any coast unless the coastal nation proved its fish were overfished. MSY was written into the 1982 UN convention on the oceans, {{ref:nature-gov-142}}, even as scientists questioned it.

nature-res-024.title: Marine protected areas: parks in the sea
nature-res-024.text: Biodiversity in fully protected marine reserves rose by an average of 23% after designation. A marine protected area (MPA) is part of the seas, oceans or estuaries where human activity is restricted for conservation. Rules vary widely, covering development, fishing methods, seasons, catch limits and bans on disturbing marine life. Not all MPAs ban fishing: less than 1 percent of US waters are no-take zones. Meta-analyses show no-take reserves give the biggest ecological benefits, especially when well monitored, over ten years old and suitably sized. MPAs can also help fishing by letting stocks recover, and create jobs through ecotourism; a 2024 meta-analysis found no net cost to fisheries across 24 countries. Yet in 2020 only about 7.5 to 8% of the global ocean was under a conservation designation. Some MPAs are criticized by indigenous communities for impinging on their land-use rights.

nature-res-080.title: Marine conservation: managing the seas so they last
nature-res-080.text: Baleen whales were nearing extinction when the International Whaling Commission's global ban on commercial whaling took effect in 1986. Marine conservation is the protection of ocean and sea ecosystems through planned management, so that marine resources are not over-exploited. It aims to limit human damage, restore damaged ecosystems and preserve vulnerable species. It draws on marine biology, ecology, oceanography and the science of fisheries, together with economics, maritime law and policy. Its tools include reserves with seasonal or permanent closures and zoning, sustainable fisheries and fishing quotas. Overfishing is one of the main causes of declining ocean wildlife: the FAO reported sustainable stocks fell from 90% in 1974 to 65.8% in 2017. Researchers suggest blending in customary local management, though past attempts to combine the two have often failed.

nature-res-061.title: How fished populations grow and shrink
nature-res-061.text: In 1838 Pierre Verhulst wrote down an equation in which growth slows as numbers approach a ceiling, the carrying capacity K. Fisheries scientists still use that logistic equation. The population dynamics of fisheries studies how a fished population grows and shrinks over time through births, deaths and migration. Its purpose is practical: to work out sustainable yields and the best harvesting rates. Under logistic growth, maximum sustainable yield sits at exactly half the carrying capacity, where the population grows fastest. Schaefer's catch equation makes the catch proportional to fishing effort, times stock biomass, times a catchability factor. The Baranov catch equation of 1918 is perhaps the most used equation in fisheries modeling. And the field's first principle is widely held to be Malthus's exponential law.

nature-res-041.title: Bycatch: the fish nobody wanted
nature-res-041.text: An estimated 100,000 albatross a year die on fishing longlines. Bycatch is fish or other marine life caught unintentionally while fishing for particular species or sizes. It may be the wrong species, the wrong sex, or undersized young of the target species. It makes up about a quarter of all marine catch and is usually thrown back to die. Shrimp trawls show the extreme: they take two percent of the world's catch by weight but produce over one-third of all bycatch. Gillnets, longlines and bottom trawls cause most of it, including dolphins, sea turtles and seabirds. Remedies include closing areas with high bycatch and changing gear. Norway's policy of no throwing back makes fishers keep everything they catch.

nature-res-047.title: Exclusive economic zones: owning the sea off the coast
nature-res-047.text: Territorial waters once reached only 3 nautical miles from shore, the range of a cannon shot. Today an exclusive economic zone (EEZ) stretches from the edge of territorial waters at 12 nautical miles out to 200. Set by the 1982 UN convention on the oceans, part of {{ref:nature-gov-142}}, it gives a coastal state exclusive rights to explore and use marine resources there. EEZs were introduced to end heated clashes over fishing rights, as oil also grew important. About one-third of the ocean now lies within them. Boundaries still cause conflict; the UK–Iceland Cod Wars ended with a 1976 agreement. Fish that cross EEZ boundaries, transboundary stocks, are key to controlling catches. Beyond the zones fishing is hard to control, and most high-seas fisheries survive only on subsidies.

nature-res-057.title: Illegal, unreported and unregulated fishing
nature-res-057.text: In some important fisheries, as much as 30% of the catch is illegal, unreported or unregulated. This IUU fishing covers fishing without permission or against the law, fishing that is not reported or wrongly reported, and fishing where no conservation rules apply. It is thought to occur in most fisheries. It costs the global economy between $10 billion and $23 billion a year, making it among the most profitable natural resource crimes. Its harms include biodiversity loss, habitat damage from illegal methods, overfishing and bycatch. Illegal and unreported fishing arise mainly from failure to enforce existing laws, often rooted in poor national governance. Where rights in small-scale fisheries are weakly enforced, free-riding and illegal fishing follow. Mandatory certification and catch documentation increasingly keep IUU products out of markets.

nature-res-016.title: Fisheries science: the study behind the catch
nature-res-016.text: Michael Graham's 'Great Law of Fishing' holds that unlimited fisheries become unprofitable. Fisheries science is the academic discipline of understanding and managing fisheries. It draws on oceanography, marine and freshwater biology, ecology, population dynamics, economics, statistics and decision analysis. Research vessels tow nets, sample plankton and water, and carry acoustic fish-finders. Fedor Baranov's 1918 catch equation is perhaps the most used equation in fisheries modeling. New fields have grown out of the discipline, such as bioeconomics and {{ref:nature-res-036}}.

nature-res-077.title: Wild fisheries: humanity's last big wild food
nature-res-077.text: Fish farming is growing, yet most fish people eat still comes from the wild. Wild fisheries, also called capture fisheries, are natural waters holding free-ranging fish or shellfish caught for commercial value. They are humanity's only significant wild food source. They can be marine or freshwater, and they depend heavily on the carrying capacity of the local ecosystem. Upwellings bring nutrients that feed plankton-eating forage fish, which draw larger predators; the Humboldt Current supports a significant share of the world catch. Significant wild fisheries have collapsed or are close to it, through overfishing and pollution. Pollution, eutrophication and ocean acidification, which may weaken shellfish shells and corals, all threaten them. Global wild fisheries are believed to have peaked and begun to decline.

nature-res-032.title: Open access: how competition wipes out a fishery's profit
nature-res-032.text: In an open fishery, a fisher who wants a bigger catch can only take it from someone else's share, since no one can be kept out. Competition then drives fishers to invest in boats and gear until their costs equal their revenue, and the resource rent is wiped out. Gordon showed that overexploitation and this rent dissipation spring from the property rights regime itself. Fish also move across borders, so one country's conservation can be exploited by another. The industry's financial stake fuels lobbying that can block or weaken policy against overfishing. The tragedy of the commons can even create perverse incentives for more subsidies.

nature-res-028.title: Three ways to overfish
nature-res-028.text: Biologists recognize three types of overfishing, each striking a different part of the system. Growth overfishing catches fish too young. They are smaller, on average, than the size that gives the most yield per young fish entering the stock, so total yield is lower than it could be. Recruitment overfishing goes deeper. It depletes the spawning adults until too few remain to replenish the stock with new young fish. Managers treat it with moratoriums, quotas and minimum size limits to rebuild the spawning biomass. Ecosystem overfishing works at the largest scale. As large predators decline, the ecosystem shifts toward small forage species.

nature-res-035.title: Climate change and fisheries: fish on the move
nature-res-035.text: Fish provides essential nutrition to 3 billion people, and a warming ocean is changing where that fish lives. Climate change affects fisheries through warming, acidifying and oxygen-poor oceans, and through altered temperatures, flows and habitats in fresh waters. It is shifting where species live and how productive they are, changing the availability and trade of fish products. Global ocean catch is expected to fall 6 percent by 2100, and 11 percent in tropical zones. The biggest falls in maximum catch potential are expected in the tropics, mostly in the South Pacific. Acidification makes it harder for shellfish, corals and zooplankton to build shells, putting 'cracks in the food chain'. Overfished stocks, smaller and less genetically diverse, are more sensitive to climate stress. Poor, rural fishing communities are the most exposed. Fishing also adds to the problem: vessels caused about 0.5 percent of global CO2 emissions in 2012, 172.3 million tonnes. Cutting fleet overcapacity and rebuilding stocks could raise resilience and returns by US$50 billion a year, and removing fuel subsidies cuts both emissions and overfishing.

nature-res-002.title: What economists want from a fishery
nature-res-002.text: In 1954 H. Scott Gordon asked why fisheries so often ran down, and in 1955 Anthony D. Scott followed; both articles appeared in the Journal of Political Economy. Economists define the goal of fisheries management as maximizing the present value of all future profits from a fishery. They often treat fisheries as common property resources, which suffer the problems of open access, chiefly overexploitation. Gordon showed that without intervention, fishers keep entering until total value minus costs is zero, so profits vanish. The two papers became foundational for environmental economics, giving the basic case for managing renewable resources. A main remedy for this market failure is to assign property rights, which the broadest economic survey suggests prevents population collapse. Newer models add differing technologies and costs among fishers, uncertainty and the biology of how fish populations grow.

nature-res-005.title: Managing the whole ecosystem, not one fish
nature-res-005.text: A 2007 set of 'ten commandments' urged managers to keep big old females, natural stock boundaries, seafloor habitats and food-web links. That is the spirit of ecosystem-based fisheries management, which manages fishing for the health and productivity of the whole ecosystem rather than single target species. It is organized around ecosystem services. Current scientific consensus favors it as the most workable way to balance human needs, keep those services and limit ecological harm. It also asks managers to adapt to climate change, account for evolution driven by fishing, and include human social and economic systems. Pitcher and Pauly go further. Harvesting simplifies ecosystems toward small, low-level species, they argue, so the goal should be rebuilding ecosystems, not sustainability as such.

nature-res-003.title: Controlling what goes in and what comes out
nature-res-003.text: Every fishing rule limits one of two things: what goes into fishing, such as boats and gear, or what comes out, the catch. Fisheries regulation falls into four core categories, depending also on whether that limit is direct or indirect. Licensing vessels is an indirect input control. Limiting entry to the fishery is a direct input control. On the output side, rules on catching techniques or equipment act indirectly, while catch quotas with technical regulation act directly. Technical measures include minimum mesh sizes, bans on certain nets or weapons, and limits on vessel numbers and time at sea. Many countries run fisheries ministries that apply these controls within their exclusive economic zones.

nature-res-066.title: Recreational fishing: a hobby worth billions
nature-res-066.text: In 2014, about 11 million saltwater anglers in the United States generated $58 billion in sales impacts. Recreational fishing, also called sport or game fishing, is fishing for leisure, exercise or competition rather than profit or survival. Its most common form is angling, with rod, reel, line, hooks and bait. It is old: the earliest English essay on it appeared in 1496, and Izaak Walton wrote The Compleat Angler in 1653. Governments set licenses and rules on lures, bait and hooks to keep it sustainable, and many anglers voluntarily practice catch and release. Stocking non-native fish for sport has harmed aquatic life and made freshwater fish communities more alike. Policy makers have largely ignored the sector, though a framework now exists to give it the attention commercial fisheries get.

nature-res-060.title: Optimum sustainable yield: the most profitable catch
nature-res-060.text: Fishing as hard as biology allows is rarely the most profitable choice. Optimum sustainable yield is the level of fishing effort that maximizes the gap between total revenue and total cost, the resource's economic profit or rent. At that level, marginal revenue equals marginal cost. It usually means less effort than maximum sustainable yield. In environmental science, it is the largest economic yield a renewable resource can give over a long period without weakening the population's ability to keep supplying it. Knowing mortality rates helps managers set harvest limits at either level.

nature-res-054.title: Fishing down the food web
nature-res-054.text: In pristine oceans, the biomass of large predators was 10 to 100 times greater than today. Over the last 50 years alone, cod, swordfish, tuna and other large predators have dropped 90 percent in abundance. In fishing down the food web, fisheries that have used up the big predators turn to smaller species. Finally they take small fish and invertebrates once ignored. Daniel Pauly and colleagues first demonstrated it in a 1998 article in Science. The logic is simple. Bigger fish usually sit higher in the food chain, and fishing tends to take bigger fish, so intense fishing leaves small fish dominating catches. Using {{ref:nature-res-006}} modeling, Pauly found the average trophic level of catches fell by between 0.5 and 1.0 levels over 50 years, globally and in each ocean. Rising prices for small forage fish and invertebrates can be seen as subsidizing the slide. The finding is contested. FAO scientists argued Pauly's team misread the catch statistics. Later studies attribute the falling levels to added low-level fisheries or climate swings rather than predator collapse, and find it is not a global phenomenon.

nature-res-052.title: Fisheries subsidies: paying fleets to fish
nature-res-052.text: Governments spend an estimated US$15–35 billion a year on fisheries subsidies. A fisheries subsidy gives fishers or fish consumers an advantage by topping up their income or lowering their costs. Forms include direct payments, price support, tax breaks, low-interest loans and preferential treatment. Some subsidies support conservation, but others threaten stocks by encouraging too many boats and too much fishing. They are estimated to leave the industry earning US$ 50 billion less per year than it could. In 2022 the WTO ordered an end to subsidies for illegal fishing, fishing in international waters and fishing of overfished stocks. Target 14.6 of {{ref:nature-gov-027}} aims to prohibit subsidies that drive overcapacity and overfishing.

openers.fisheries: About 500 million people depend on fisheries for their living, and fish feed billions more. Fish stocks are renewable, but only while they are caught no faster than they can breed, and many are not. This chapter follows the science and economics of fishing: how a stock grows, how much can be taken year after year, and why open access drives fleets to take too much. It then turns to the tools that answer that pressure, from catch limits and protected areas to exclusive zones at sea and quotas that fishers can own.
